description_ru: Размышление о том, почему постоянное развлечение мешает творчеству и почему детям (и взрослым) полезно иногда скучать.
text:
Last summer I made a small experiment. For one afternoon I left my phone at home, took a train to the coast and sat on a bench with nothing to read, watch or listen to. The first twenty minutes were almost painful. My hand kept reaching for a pocket that was empty, and I felt strangely guilty, as if I were wasting my time. Then something changed. I noticed the colour of the water, a man walking a very small dog, a conversation I would have missed. By the end of the afternoon I had solved a problem at work that had been bothering me for a week.

This experience is not unusual, and psychologists have studied it. When our minds are not occupied with a task, the brain does not switch off. Instead it becomes active in a different way, linking memories, imagining the future and making unexpected connections. Researchers call this the default network. It is during these quiet moments that we are most likely to have a creative idea, to understand how we really feel or to plan the next stage of our lives. The trouble is that we have almost eliminated such moments from daily life.

Think about how rarely we are left alone with our thoughts. We check our phones in the queue at the supermarket, in the lift, on the toilet. Waiting for a bus used to mean staring into space, and now it means scrolling through news we will forget in five minutes. One study found that many people, when asked to sit in an empty room for a quarter of an hour, preferred to give themselves mild electric shocks rather than do nothing. That result astonished me. It suggests that boredom is not just unpleasant for us, it is almost unbearable.

Children are especially affected. Parents today are under strong pressure to keep their children busy and happy, with an endless supply of lessons, clubs and screens. A mother I know told me that she felt like a failure whenever her daughter complained that she had nothing to do. But a famous educator once said that boredom is the beginning of invention. When a child has nothing to do, she has to build a den from cushions, write a story, or stare at an ant for half an hour. These activities may look pointless, yet they are the training ground of imagination.

Many great minds seem to have understood this. Writers have described how their best ideas arrived on a long walk or in the bath. It is said that a famous physicist came up with an important insight while he was riding on a tram. Another popular anecdote, which may or may not be true, claims that a scientist found the shape of a molecule after dozing in front of the fire. I would not stake my life on such stories, but they all point in the same direction: a restless mind needs gaps.

Naturally, I am not suggesting that we should throw away our phones or that entertainment is a sin. I love a good film as much as anyone, and a long journey with a podcast can be a real pleasure. The problem is the constant, automatic reaching for stimulation. It trains us to expect a reward every few seconds and makes ordinary life seem dull. If a book seems too slow or a conversation too quiet, the fault may lie not with the book or the person but with a brain that has been overfed with sugar.

There is also a social cost. When people are bored together, they talk. A long car journey, a rainy day in a holiday cottage or a delayed flight can produce the best conversations of a lifetime. Now every member of the family is often looking at a different screen, and the opportunity is lost. Some families have started to introduce phone-free dinners and screen-free Sundays. They report that the first week is difficult and that afterwards, to their surprise, they do not want to go back.

So what can we do? Start small. Leave your phone in your bag on the way to work. Walk without headphones. Let a child complain that there is nothing to do, and resist the temptation to rescue her. Learn to sit in a waiting room and simply watch the people. None of this needs money or special equipment, and the rewards are immediate: a calmer mind, a longer attention span, and perhaps a good idea or two.

Boredom has a bad reputation, but I have come to think of it as a kind of fallow field, which looks empty but is quietly preparing for the next harvest. If we cover every inch with entertainment, nothing will have room to grow. The next time you find yourself with nothing to do, I hope you will resist the urge to reach for your phone and let the silence do its work.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Тот же положение языка, что для θ, но с голосом: звук гудит, не «з».
Губы округлены вперёд, без касания зубами; не путайте с «в».
Ударение ставьте на нужный слог: ударный слог длиннее, громче и выше по тону, остальные сокращаются.
Задняя часть языка к мягкому нёбу, звук идёт через нос; не добавляйте «г» в конце.

questions.question: What did the author do on the experimental afternoon?
questions.answer: Left the phone at home and sat on a bench by the sea with nothing to do.

questions.question: What do psychologists say the brain does when we are not busy?
questions.answer: It stays active, linking memories and making unexpected connections.

questions.question: Why is boredom good for children?
questions.answer: It makes them invent games and use imagination.

questions.question: What simple steps does the author suggest?
questions.answer: Leave the phone in the bag, walk without headphones, let children be bored.
